title: Construction of Geometric Figures
summary: Construct special angles, parallel and perpendicular lines and triangle bisectors with a compass and ruler, and use constructions to investigate the diagonals of quadrilaterals, the angle sum of polygons and the conditions for congruent triangles.

notes.text: Constructions you should be able to do

items: Bisect a line segment (perpendicular bisector) and bisect an angle.
Construct a perpendicular from a point on a line, and from a point not on a line.
Construct angles of $60^\circ$ (equilateral triangle) and $90^\circ$ (perpendicular), and by bisecting, $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $15^\circ$.
Construct triangles (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) and quadrilaterals from given information.

notes.title: Worked example 1: a 75° angle
notes.problem: Describe how to construct an angle of $75^\circ$ at point $A$ on a line, without a protractor.
steps: Construct a $60^\circ$ angle at $A$ (arc from $A$ cutting the line at $B$; same width from $B$ gives $C$; draw $AC$).
Construct a perpendicular at $A$, giving a $90^\circ$ angle on the same side.
The angle between the $60^\circ$ arm and the $90^\circ$ arm is $30^\circ$. Bisect it to get two $15^\circ$ angles.
The bisector makes $60^\circ + 15^\circ = 75^\circ$ with the line.
notes.answer: Construct 60° and 90°, then bisect the 30° between them.

items: Given line $AB$ and point $P$ not on it, draw any line through $P$ that crosses $AB$ at $Q$.
At $Q$, the line $PQ$ makes an angle with $AB$. Draw an arc centred at $Q$ cutting both lines.
With the same compass width, draw an arc centred at $P$.
Measure the opening of the first arc with the compass and transfer it to the arc at $P$, so that you **copy the angle** in the corresponding position.
Draw the line through $P$ and the new point. It is parallel to $AB$, because corresponding angles are equal.

notes.text: If you construct the **perpendicular bisectors** of all three sides of a triangle, they meet at one point, the **circumcentre**. It is the same distance from all three vertices, so a circle centred there passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$ (the circumscribed circle). The **angle bisectors** of a triangle also meet at one point, the **incentre**, which is the centre of the circle that touches all three sides.

notes.caption: The perpendicular bisectors (dashed) of the sides of triangle ABC meet at O, the circumcentre. The circle centred at O passes through A, B and C.

notes.label: Why does it work?
notes.text: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is the same distance from $A$ and $B$. The point $O$ lies on two such bisectors, so $OA = OB$ and $OB = OC$. Therefore it also lies on the third bisector.
Construct each quadrilateral accurately, draw both diagonals, and measure. You will find:

notes.caption: Properties of diagonals
rows: Only the shorter one is bisected

notes.text: Choose one vertex of a polygon with $n$ sides and draw all the diagonals from it. They divide the polygon into $n - 2$ triangles, and each triangle has angles adding up to $180^\circ$.

notes.caption: Interior angle sum of a polygon with n sides

notes.title: Worked example 2
notes.problem:
(a) A polygon has an interior angle sum of $1\ 440^\circ$. How many sides does it have?
(b) Find one exterior angle of a regular hexagon.
steps: (b) Each interior angle is $120^\circ$, so each exterior angle is $180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$. (The exterior angles of any polygon add up to $360^\circ$, and $360^\circ \div 6 = 60^\circ$.)

notes.text: By trying to construct triangles from given information, you find that two triangles are congruent if they have: three sides equal (SSS); two sides and the included angle equal (SAS); two angles and a corresponding side equal (AAS); or a right angle, hypotenuse and one side equal (RHS).

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: SSA (two sides and an angle that is **not** between them) is not enough: two different triangles can often be constructed. AAA is also not enough: it gives similar triangles of any size.

items: Special angles come from $60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ by bisecting, adding and subtracting.
Copy an angle to construct a parallel line (equal corresponding angles).
Perpendicular bisectors of a triangle meet at the circumcentre; angle bisectors meet at the incentre.
Know the diagonal properties of every special quadrilateral.
Interior angle sum of an $n$-gon: $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$; exterior angles add to $360^\circ$.
Congruence: SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS (not SSA or AAA).

questions.prompt: Calculate the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon, in degrees.
The three angle bisectors of a triangle meet at a point. What is special about this point?
options: It is the midpoint of the longest side
It is the centre of the circle that touches all three sides
It is the centre of the circle through the three vertices
It is always outside the triangle
questions.explanation: The angle bisectors meet at the incentre, the centre of the inscribed circle. Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre.

questions.prompt: How can you construct an angle of $15^\circ$?
questions.explanation: Construct $60^\circ$, bisect to $30^\circ$, and bisect again to get $15^\circ$.

questions.prompt: The diagonals of every parallelogram are perpendicular.
questions.explanation: A parallelogram's diagonals bisect each other, but they are only perpendicular in special cases (rhombus, square).

questions.prompt: Match each quadrilateral with the property of its diagonals.

pairs.right: Equal, and bisect each other at 90°

questions.explanation: Each special quadrilateral adds properties to the parallelogram's.

Calculate one exterior angle of a regular hexagon, in degrees.
Which information does NOT guarantee that two triangles are congruent?
questions.explanation: With SSA, two different triangles can sometimes be constructed.

questions.prompt: Describe how to construct a line through point $P$ parallel to line $AB$, using only a compass and a ruler. Explain why the lines are parallel.
questions.memo:
Draw a line through $P$ cutting $AB$ at $Q$ ✓ (1)
Arc centred at $Q$ cutting both lines; same arc centred at $P$ ✓ (1)
Copy the angle at $Q$ to $P$ in the corresponding position and draw the line ✓ (1)
The corresponding angles are equal, so the lines are parallel ✓ (1)

questions.prompt: Explain why the sum of the interior angles of a polygon with $n$ sides is $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$.
questions.memo:
Draw all diagonals from one vertex ✓ (1)
This divides the polygon into $n - 2$ triangles ✓ (1)
Each triangle has an angle sum of $180^\circ$, so the total is $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$ ✓ (1)

questions.prompt: Describe how to construct an angle of $75^\circ$ at a point $A$ on a line, using only a compass and a ruler.
questions.memo:
Construct a $60^\circ$ angle at $A$ ✓ (1)
Construct a $90^\circ$ angle (perpendicular) at $A$ on the same side ✓ (1)
Bisect the $30^\circ$ angle between them: $60^\circ + 15^\circ = 75^\circ$ ✓ (1)

questions.prompt: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of $\triangle ABC$ meet at $O$. Explain why a circle centred at $O$ passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$.
questions.memo:
Any point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from its endpoints, so $OA = OB$ and $OB = OC$ ✓ (1)
So $OA = OB = OC$, and a circle with radius $OA$ passes through all three vertices ✓ (1)
